body: Monday, June 29 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed remains on hold in a hawkish posture. The 2Y yield at 4.07% (prior close) is rising (+8 bps vs 4W), while the 10Y at 4.38% is slightly falling (−7 bps vs 4W) — the curve is flattening from the front end, which is a classic "hawkish hold + growth deceleration" signal. The 10Y-2Y spread at +31 bps is positive but still flat by historical standards, and narrowing. VIX at 17.86 is up 16.6% from four weeks ago — complacency is eroding. Borrowed money fueling equities is getting more expensive per Reuters. The S&P 500 at 7420 is down 2.1% vs 4W; Nasdaq down 2.2%.

New / Most Important: The Supreme Court blocked Trump from firing Fed Governor Lisa Cook, preserving Fed independence for now. This is structurally significant: the Humphrey's Executor doctrine is trending alongside SCOTUS, signaling the market is watching executive-vs-independent-agency power dynamics in real time. If the Court ultimately rules that the President can fire Fed board members at will, it would represent the most consequential change to US monetary governance since 1935 — effectively politicizing rate-setting and introducing a permanent political risk premium into the long end of the curve. The fact that this was a temporary block, not a final ruling, means the tail risk persists. Additionally, BIS warned that the AI investment boom could trigger a stock market slump and jeopardize the broader economy — the central bank of central banks is now formally on record with this concern. Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) opened the door to Bitcoin sales, a first crack in what had been a one-directional BTC treasury model.

Playbook ✓: Rotation from mega-cap tech to small caps is proceeding as expected — Russell 2000 up 2.5% vs Nasdaq down 2.2%, Russell/Nasdaq ratio up 4.8%. The "healthy rotation" narrative from Invesco aligns with breadth expansion.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The divergence is in the risk-pricing complex. Gold is down 11.4% vs 4W — a massive drawdown for the "flight to quality" asset — even as the growth pulse softens: May housing starts fell to their weakest since 2020, new home sales hit a four-month low and the June flash PMI showed factory jobs at their lowest since 2020. The resolution likely lies in a liquidity squeeze — real rates are rising (per the "rising real rates reshape markets" headline), forcing leveraged gold longs to liquidate just as rate-sensitive demand weakens. This is not a risk-on signal; it's a simultaneous de-risking of both safe-haven and cyclical positions, which historically precedes either a sharp policy pivot or a credit event.

Macro Stance: The ECB is in an ambiguous spot — consumer inflation expectations cooled to 3.5% per the ECB's own survey, but Schnabel warned the ECB may need to raise rates further. Spanish inflation held above the ECB's target. The euro has remained stronger despite mixed ECB commentary. Bulgaria joined the euro, a milestone for eurozone expansion.

New / Most Important: Schnabel's hawkish warning is the headline — this is the ECB's most influential hawk publicly floating further hikes even as consumer expectations are falling. Spain's sticky inflation provides cover for the hawk camp. Bulgaria's euro accession, while symbolic, marginally expands the eurozone's monetary base and creates a small structural bid for euro-denominated assets from the rebalancing of Bulgarian reserves.

Playbook ✓: Core-periphery inflation divergence continues — Spain sticky, Northern Europe cooler. Bond investors are being told by Morningstar to position cautiously for Q3.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Consumer inflation expectations declining while a key ECB policymaker flags more hikes is a classic late-cycle central bank credibility gap. If the ECB hikes into falling expectations, it risks an overtightening accident, particularly for Southern European sovereigns where fiscal dynamics are less forgiving.

Macro Stance: The PBOC is rebuilding its operating framework rather than cutting. Loan prime rates were held for a 13th month in June (Business Times, [Jun 22]), and over the weekend the bank debuted its overnight reverse repo at 1.25%, according to sources (Reuters, [Jun 28]), below the 1.35% a survey had pointed to (Bloomberg, [Jun 25]). That is easing at the very front end by framework, not by headline cut. The yuan fixing was weakened for a fourth session as the dollar advanced (Bloomberg, [Jun 23]): a managed drift lower against a dollar at 13-month highs, while the ECB openly calls the yuan undervalued (Reuters, [Jun 22]); T. Rowe Price sees it falling 1%-2% by year-end (TradingView, [Jun 26]). Prices are split: May CPI rose only 1.2% (China Daily, [Jun 10]) while factory-gate inflation hit a near four-year high (Reuters, [Jun 9]).

PMIs & Activity: The official manufacturing PMI stalled at 50 in May (Reuters, [May 30]) with factory orders contracting (Wood Central, [Jun 1]), and the non-manufacturing gauge was barely positive at 50.1 (Macau Business, [May 31]). Private surveys were firmer, with services at 54.4 (TradingView, [Jun 2]), and a Reuters poll sees June factory activity returning only to meagre growth ([Jun 28]). Industrial output growth quickened to 4.5% in May (China Daily, [Jun 16]), but retail sales fell 0.6%, the first drop in over three years (Il Sole 24 Ore, [Jun 15]), and fixed-asset investment was down 4.1% in the first five months (Macau Business, [Jun 16]). Industrial profits rose 18.8% in January–May (WSJ, [Jun 26]) and but profit growth slowed for the first time in six months as weak domestic demand bit (Times of India, [Jun 27]).

Credit Impulse: Total social financing grew 7.7% in May (CGTN, [Jun 12]) and topped forecasts (Bloomberg, [Jun 12]), but new loans missed as the property slump curbed demand (Reuters, [Jun 12]). The beat is government-bond issuance; private credit demand is still contracting. The PBOC is now urging banks to boost lending because demand remains weak, according to sources (Reuters, [Jun 26]). Household deleveraging continues (SCMP, [Jun 15]). Read: the headline impulse is flat-to-positive, but the household and private-firm impulse is still negative, which is why output does not convert into consumption.

Property: New home prices fell at a faster pace in May (Reuters, [Jun 15]) even as first-tier new home prices rose for a third month (SCMP, [Jun 16]) and top-city resale prices extended their rebound (Caixin, [Jun 17]). Real-estate investment fell 16.2% y/y in January–May (GMK Center, [Jun 18]). This week the stress resurfaced at the developer level: Beijing land sales plunged 66% as developers chase only "safe" prime plots (Caixin, [Jun 25]), and the Evergrande Property Services stake sale collapsed, sending its shares down 24% (Caixin, [Jun 26]). The Straits Times describes steel entering a long plateau after the property crash ([Jun 22]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: The fiscal signal is the surprise. Beijing narrowed its cumulative deficit for the first time since 2023 (Bloomberg, [Jun 22]). A third batch of 62.5 billion yuan for consumer-goods trade-ins was allocated (Global Times, [Jun 26]): targeted support, small relative to the retail contraction. Exports jumped 19.4% in May (AP, [Jun 9]) and shipments to the US grew 35% (CNBC, [Jun 8]). Beijing says it can withstand an EU trade freeze (Bloomberg, [Jun 28]), and German carmakers are embarking on historic job cuts as Chinese rivals flood the market (Financial Times, [Jun 27]). Beijing hit 10 US firms, including MP Materials, with export controls (Reuters, [Jun 22]), and the 55% tariff on Australian beef is now in force (Australian Rural & Regional News, [Jun 22]).

Markets & Flows: Onshore and offshore have decoupled. Mainland stocks hit a 4-1/2-year high (TradingView, [Jun 22]), led by AI names on demand optimism and policy support (Business Times, [Jun 22]). Hong Kong is the opposite: the HSCEI entered a technical bear market (finance.biggo.com, [Jun 23]), Bloomberg ties the slide to spending woes ([Jun 23]), and the Hang Seng capped its worst week in over a year amid a tech sell-off (SCMP, [Jun 26]). The Hang Seng Tech index rebounded nearly 4% as Baidu's Kunlun chip unit eyed a $50 billion Hong Kong IPO (finance.biggo.com, [Jun 28]),. CITIC Securities' acknowledgement that Hong Kong has significantly underperformed other Asian markets this year is a capital-flow red flag: the rebound is AI issuance, not a consumer re-rating.

New / Most Important: The 1.25% overnight rate is the first concrete easing step of the new framework, and it came in below expectations. It lands as government advisers call for a fix to the two-speed economy (Bloomberg, [Jun 27]) and the PBOC urges banks to lend into weak demand. Cheaper overnight money helps bond and equity financing, the channels the AI sector uses, but not households. With new loans missing and the first fiscal-gap cutback since 2023, the credit impulse that matters for households is not turning. Until Beijing reverses the fiscal tightening, growth leans on exports, and Europe is closing the gates (economy.ac, [Jun 28]).

Playbook ✓: Property drag, weak consumption, LPR on hold and a managed yuan drift lower are all on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The consensus expected a mid-year stimulus pivot; instead the credit impulse outside government bonds is negative and the fiscal impulse is narrowing. China is therefore exporting its excess supply rather than absorbing it at home. The transmission runs through three channels. European exporters face a widening bilateral deficit and a weak yuan, and the auto job cuts show the damage is already in payrolls. Bulk-commodity demand tied to construction is fading, with the steel plateau and an investment slump that hit AUD alongside the beef tariff. And global goods disinflation is the channel Pimco expects to support EM bonds (Bloomberg, [Jun 23]). A real turn needs loan growth, not bond issuance, to re-accelerate; until it does, rallies in Hong Kong are flows, not fundamentals.

Macro Stance: The BOJ hiked rates recently — confirmed by multiple feed headlines — and a hawkish policymaker called for hikes "once every few months." Yet the yen continued to fall despite the hike, with an ex-BOJ policymaker warning a Fed hike could push yen to 165/USD. Intervention risk remains elevated, with Japan continuing to issue verbal warnings.

New / Most Important: This is structurally new and critical for global capital flows. The BOJ is now in an active hiking cycle — the summary of opinions affirmed the rate hike stance as inflation risks mount — yet the yen is STILL depreciating. This breaks the orthodox textbook completely. The yen problem that "Japan's rate hike couldn't solve" is fundamentally a carry trade problem: the interest rate differential with the US remains wide enough that hiking 25bps at a time does nothing to reverse the structural short-yen position embedded in global portfolios. Japanese inflation approaching the BOJ's target gives them cover to keep hiking, but they're in a bind — the pace required to defend the yen would crater JGBs and threaten domestic financial stability. The real risk is that MOF intervention becomes the only tool left, and intervention without fundamental convergence just creates vol spikes that benefit carry traders on the dip. Global macro implication: the yen carry unwind remains the single largest latent vol event in global markets.
Playbook ✓: BOJ hiking, yen weak, Nikkei gaining — all consistent with the Japan reflation trade.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The divergence IS the playbook failure — hikes aren't fixing the yen. See above.

Macro Stance: The RBA held rates at its last meeting. However, underlying inflation remains too high, keeping another rate hike on the table. Bond traders won't rule out a fourth rate rise. The RBA's Kent suggested the board may have "less tolerance for inflation" going forward, while simultaneously preparing "fire drills" for crisis scenarios.

New / Most Important: The juxtaposition is remarkable — on the same day, RBA communications suggest both that near-zero rates are "closer than you think" (AFR) AND that hikes remain on the cards. This is either deeply confused forward guidance or a deliberate attempt to anchor both tails. Kent's "less tolerance for inflation" comment is the operative signal — it tilts the next move toward a hike, not a cut. For AUD, lingering hike bets are keeping the currency supported.

Playbook ✓: Sticky inflation in a commodity-linked economy with a housing bubble is textbook for extended hawkish holds.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The "near-zero rates closer than you think" briefing is the outlier — if this reflects genuine internal modeling of a deflationary shock scenario (China hard landing?), it suggests the RBA sees a bimodal distribution of outcomes, which is itself a risk signal.

Macro Stance: The NBP's room is narrowing from the fiscal side: Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK argues the state's debt now ties the central bank's hands [Jun 29], and the RPP is waiting (Parkiet, [Jun 25]) after a hike vote at the last meeting (Tysol.pl, [Jun 22]). The inflation calendar turns this week: Wednesday brings the return of the higher fuel VAT and a free market in fuel prices after the energy minister's last maximum-price notice (Next Gazeta.pl, [Jun 29]), petrol is already at 6 zł with diesel clearly dearer (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 29]), and Gazeta Prawna warns the energy shock will feed food prices and lift inflation in 2027 [Jun 29]. The heatwave adds to it: power prices jumped over 500% on the exchanges (Next Gazeta.pl, [Jun 29]). Labour is cooling rather than tightening: unemployment is the lowest in months (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 24]) but employment has fallen for a 32nd consecutive month (Super Biznes, [Jun 22]) and wages show no clear acceleration (Portal spożywczy, [Jun 22]), with May pay up 5.8% y/y, below expectations (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 22]). Factories carry a record 8.6 bn zł of arrears (Strefa Biznesu, [Jun 24]) even as defence orders flood in (Business Insider Polska, [Jun 27]). The old reading of Poland as a central bank leaning toward easing no longer fits this feed.

Markets: Monday was mixed on the WIG20, with Orlen and Żabka finishing higher (Inwestycje.pl, [Jun 29]) and Rzeczpospolita noting rising geopolitical tension did not favour buying [Jun 29]. INNPoland.pl attributes Orlen's gain to Slovak expansion, renewables and geopolitics [Jun 29], while KGHM is being hit by a plunge in a key metal (wnp.pl, [Jun 29]) and silver is falling alongside gold (Money.pl, [Jun 29]). Friday's closes on the card: EPOL 38.27 (-3.7% 1W, -5.7% 4W); KGHM 327.75 (-10.3% 1W); Orlen 123.46 (-2.3% 1W, -12.6% 4W); PGE 9.6 (-11.1% 4W); Allegro 37.19 (-5.7% 1W, +8.7% 4W); CD Projekt 217.4 (-3.0% 1W); LPP 18310 (-16.4% 4W); PKO 103.62 and Pekao 228.8 (-1.6% and -2.8% 1W); Dino 28.98 (-6.6% 4W). Trigon DM moved to buy LPP and Pepco and sell Modivo (Strefa Inwestorów, [Jun 29]). FX: USD/PLN at 3.7641 (+1.5% 1W, +3.7% 4W) and EUR/PLN at 4.2855 (+0.8% 1W, +1.4% 4W); CEO Magazyn has the euro at 4.29 zł with the dollar losing and investors cautious on the zloty [Jun 29], while Business Insider Polska sees the dollar regaining strength and the zloty on the defensive [Jun 29]. Bonds: servicing costs are up almost 30% (Parkiet, [Jun 25]) and FXMAG raises the risk of Poland being cut off from EU funds over the state of its finances [Jun 29].

Fiscal & Politics: The windfall tax escalated again: a Senate amendment means the maximum levy could reach 100% of profit (Strefa Inwestorów, [Jun 29]), on top of the 74% safety valve reported last week (Wyborcza.biz, [Jun 26]) and the Sejm's 60% base (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 19]); Money.pl carries an economist urging Poland to change the tax, citing Hungary [Jun 29]. Rzeczpospolita says it is time to review state spending [Jun 29] after Bankier.pl flagged a pile-up of outlays on nuclear and CPK with an EU procedure in the background [Jun 27] and debt growth of 1.5 bn zł a day (wPolityce.pl, [Jun 26]). The promised pension recalculation is stuck in government (Fakt, [Jun 29]), and MF confirmed a three-euro customs charge on non-EU parcels from the start of July (Prawo.pl, [Jun 29]). The CHF law awaits the president's signature after the Senate passed it unamended (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 25]).

Corporate & Sectors: PKO BP shareholders approved a dividend of 6.14 zł per share from 2025 profit (Bankier.pl, [Jun 29]), a raise for the country's largest bank (Business Insider Polska, [Jun 29]); the sector context is tougher, with Polish banks earning 13.3 bn zł as tax and margin pressure cut earnings (CEO Magazyn, [Jun 29]), ZBP forecasting a near 23% drop in sector profit from the free-credit sanction (Bankier.pl, [Jun 26]) and Erste Bank Polska booking over 438 mln zł of CHF legal-risk losses (Bankier.pl, [Jun 29]). Orlen pre-paid the higher VAT before it took effect (TOK FM, [Jun 29]), launched HVO100 fuel in Slovakia (Money.pl, [Jun 29]) and, with Synthos, applied for the EU's first contract for difference for SMRs, seeking guarantees for 14 reactors (Bankier.pl, [Jun 29]). Nuclear negotiations are intensifying toward an EPC contract (Dziennik Bałtycki, [Jun 29]). Dino's owner lost the title of richest Pole as his fortune nearly halved (WP Finanse, [Jun 29]) and the state labour inspectorate took up the staff complaints (Wiadomości Handlowe, [Jun 29]). CD Projekt dated Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 for autumn with a trailer (Antyweb, [Jun 29]), and Blik's chief is moving to Allegro (pb.pl, [Jun 29]).

Geopolitics & Security: Poland's spy chief said the country must operate as if war with Russia were imminent (TVP World, [Jun 29]) and warned Russia could use unmarked troops against the Baltic states (UNITED24 Media, [Jun 29]); the Dutch government assesses Russia could attack NATO a year after the Ukraine war ends (Kyiv Post, [Jun 29]). Saab won a Polish submarine order worth 4.3 billion dollars (Investing.com, [Jun 29]), adding to the defence-order wave.

New / Most Important: The windfall tax has gone from 60% to a theoretical 100% in ten days, in the same week the fuel VAT returns and power prices spike on the heat. That is a stagflationary policy mix for the state-controlled complex and for CPI, which is why Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK now says debt ties the NBP's hands: the market has stopped pricing a Polish easing cycle and started pricing a fiscal one. PKO's 6.14 zł dividend is the counterweight, proof that bank capital return survives the tax squeeze.  |  Playbook ✓: Hold with upside inflation risk from Wednesday; stay long PKO into the dividend, keep Orlen tactical only, and respect KGHM's metal-price drawdown rather than fading it.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Orlen shares rising on the day its tax ceiling rose to 100%; unemployment at multi-month lows while employment falls for a 32nd month; a 4.3 billion dollar submarine order against FXMAG's warning that EU funds could be cut off.

Macro Stance: Spain's 2026 growth forecast was raised to 2.6% — a periphery-Europe bright spot but not strictly EM. El Niño is being flagged as a cross-asset risk for commodity-exporting EMs (Investing.com). Iran-related geopolitical risk was shrugged off by the S&P per Seeking Alpha.

New / Most Important: El Niño's potential market impact is being discussed — historically hits agricultural commodity exporters (Brazil, Indonesia, India) and benefits certain energy names. Worth monitoring for soft commodity vol.  |  Playbook ✓: Geopolitical risk being ignored by equity markets is standard late-cycle behavior.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: None material this week.

Narrative: Consensus is split between AI boom and AI bubble: demand is real, but memory costs now bite hardware, with Apple raising prices (Investing.com, [Jun 26]) and asking to buy memory from a blacklisted supplier (AppleInsider, [Jun 27]), while the 2Y at 4.07% caps multiples.

Reported: BlackBerry lifted its annual revenue forecast as the QNX unit powered growth (BNN Bloomberg, [Jun 25]); Q1 earnings exceeded expectations and the stock climbed 20% (TradingView, [Jun 26]). TD SYNNEX beat on Q2 revenue and analysts raised targets (scanx.trade, [Jun 25]). Accenture's revenue-growth guidance cut shocked the IT services industry (The Hindu, [Jun 27]).

EPS Upside Watch: Oracle — a $638 billion AI backlog (24/7 Wall St., [Jun 23]) is contracted revenue still to convert into earnings. IBM — shares jumped 5% after JPMorgan upgraded the stock on software acceleration (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 24]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The BIS warning that the AI investment boom could trigger a market slump legitimises the bubble thesis institutionally. Its reports are read by sovereign funds and reserve managers who move hundreds of billions, giving risk managers cover to cut tech exposure.
Narrative: The platforms sit between AI-driven engagement tailwinds and the tech de-rating (Nasdaq ↓2.2% vs 4W), with mega-cap weight keeping them tied to the multiple compression.
Reported: No major reports this week.

EPS Upside Watch: Take-Two — an analyst says GTA VI could transform earnings (Benzinga, [Jun 24]), a single-title step-up in revenue and margins. PLDT — a data center REIT is seen as a boon to the Philippine telecom's balance sheet (Inquirer.net, [Jun 23]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: AI is usually framed as a tailwind for the ad platforms, but OpenAI now wants $100bn of ad revenue (The Media Leader, [Jun 25]) — a new rival competing for the same budgets.
Narrative: A rising 2Y (+8 bps vs 4W) lifts asset yields and a +31 bps curve, though thin, supports net interest margins; credit quality is the swing factor, as Judo's bad loans show.

Reported: Jefferies' quarterly profit missed estimates as asset management weighed (Reuters, [Jun 24]), despite record investment-banking revenue (Quiver Quantitative, [Jun 25]). Australia's Judo Capital cut FY26 profit guidance after three loans went bad (Stocks Down Under, [Jun 25]) and the shares tanked (AFR, [Jun 25]).

EPS Upside Watch: Standard Chartered — upgraded by Deutsche Bank as the Asian wealth boom drives its earnings outlook (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 23]). Higher-for-longer US rates could also lift Singapore banks' earnings beyond 2026 (The Business Times, [Jun 25]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The Supreme Court's temporary block on firing Lisa Cook is a positive most are not pricing. Preserved Fed independence keeps the long-end term premium anchored; overturning it would reprice the whole curve and put bank balance-sheet management under stress.

Narrative: WTI at $70.78 (↓19% vs 4W) is the month's dominant cross-asset move and cuts upstream earnings, and Trump's call for a DOJ price-gouging probe of oil companies (24/7 Wall St., [Jun 24]) adds political risk.

Reported: Worley, the engineering contractor to the energy and resources industries, issued a fresh profit warning (AFR, [Jun 25]). Oil-tanker earnings plunged by $200,000 as more vessels returned to Hormuz (Bloomberg.com, [Jun 26]).

EPS Upside Watch: Big oil's trading arms — the majors' secretive trading desks are having an extraordinary year (The Economist, [Jun 28]), a profit source beyond upstream prices. BPCL and IOC — JP Morgan expects falling crude to boost Indian fuel marketers' margins (The New Indian Express, [Jun 22]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: US drillers added rigs for a fourth straight week into a 19% price collapse, a supply-discipline breakdown suggesting better breakevens or protective hedges are delaying the usual supply response. That extends the crude bear case and strains OPEC+ cohesion.

Narrative: The domestic cyclical rotation is the tailwind, with the Russell 2000 up 2.5% vs 4W, as US business activity expands on manufacturing strength (Transport Topics, [Jun 23]) and AI capex starts flowing into physical infrastructure.

Reported: FedEx beat revenue and earnings estimates yet the stock dipped 6% (TIKR.com, [Jun 24]) as it warned on inflation and trade turmoil (Bloomberg.com, [Jun 23]). Primoris Services plunged after cutting guidance on renewables cost overruns, and its COO departed (Seeking Alpha, [Jun 22]). Bunzl upgraded its outlook (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: Southwest Airlines — UBS raised its target to $61 on the earnings outlook (Investing.com, [Jun 23]). IAG — boosted as analysts cut jet fuel cost forecasts (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 22]); cheaper fuel drops straight to airline margins.
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: The consumer is K-shaped, with the rally making some rich while brick-and-mortar retail distress continues, and guidance is the weak spot: beats are met with softer outlooks as higher costs and a hawkish Fed squeeze the mass-market consumer.

Reported: Carnival posted record $6.7B revenue but the Iran war cut its cruise profit outlook (Tech Times, [Jun 24]); shares dipped 5% on weaker Q3 guidance despite the beat (TIKR.com, [Jun 24]). Darden beat but forecast annual profit below estimates on higher costs (BNN Bloomberg, [Jun 25]) as Olive Garden growth weakened (CNBC, [Jun 25]). H&M profit missed estimates (Bloomberg.com, [Jun 25]).

EPS Upside Watch: Halfords — the UK retailer sees fiscal year 2027 profit near the top end of analyst estimates (Reuters, [Jun 25]) after margins hit a decade high (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 25]). Nike reports this week (TradingKey, [Jun 28]), with its surprise CFO change seen as another tangible signal of turnaround progress (Retail Dive, [Jun 24]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: Defensive rotation should help as tech weakens, and falling oil (WTI ↓19% vs 4W) eases freight and packaging costs, but pricing rather than volume is still doing the work, which limits upside.

Reported: McCormick topped profit estimates on higher pricing (Reuters, [Jun 25]) as organic sales grew (TradingView, [Jun 25]). Couche-Tard beat estimates on strong fuel margins (BNN Bloomberg, [Jun 23]), delivering its 'best performance in years' in the US, its CEO said (C-Store Dive, [Jun 24]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged; Constellation Brands' Q1 report is next (TradingView, [Jun 25]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.
Narrative: Defensives should draw flows as the VIX (17.86) climbs and rotation broadens, but a 10Y at 4.38% and a hawkish Fed keep a lid on multiples.
Reported: No major reports this week.

EPS Upside Watch: Hims — the cash-pay telehealth platform's obesity-drug business may get a boost as employers drop coverage (Reuters, [Jun 25]). Dr Reddy's — Nomura sees 35% upside after its strategic consumer-health pivot (The Financial Express, [Jun 23]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: Gold is down 11.4% and copper 3.1% vs 4W, and copper's AI data-centre and grid-build demand case is not enough to offset a hawkish Fed. For construction materials, China is the drag, with real-estate investment down 16.2% y/y in January–May.

Reported: Evonik raised its 2026 outlook after a strong second-quarter earnings surge (Indian Chemical News, [Jun 27]), citing higher prices and cost reductions (WSJ, [Jun 26]). UK chemicals group Synthomer beat Q2 expectations and its shares surged 8% (Global Banking & Finance Review, [Jun 22]).
EPS Upside Watch: Satellite Chemical — forecasts first-half net profit surging over 118% to a record, as its ethane-based route crushes oil-based rivals on cost (finance.biggo.com, [Jun 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold's 11.4% drawdown alongside softening housing and factory-jobs data is the anomaly: a gold slump normally signals risk-on, but here it points to liquidity leaving all assets — an everything-sell-off precursor.

Narrative: Sell-side conviction is building, with Truist raising its Equity Residential target and Wells Fargo upgrading Invitation Homes to overweight, as a 10Y at 4.38% (−7 bps vs 4W) eases cap-rate pressure and homebuilder stocks show newfound technical strength (Barron's, [Jun 26]), even with mortgage rates near 6.5% (Realtor.com, [Jun 25]).

Reported: KB Home's Q2 earnings met estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 23]) and the stock jumped (The Motley Fool, [Jun 24]), even as revenue fell in a difficult housing market (WSJ, [Jun 23]). UK homebuilder Berkeley called for a tax and regulatory rethink after a 15% profit fall (Reuters, [Jun 24]).

EPS Upside Watch: Industrial REITs — MBSB sees them benefiting from data centre spin-offs and acquisitions (EdgeProp, [Jun 24]). Axis REIT — analysts call its latest purchase earnings-accretive (The Edge Malaysia, [Jun 26]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today — the upgrade cluster is consensus-confirming.
Narrative: AI data-centre power demand is the secular driver, with defensive appeal as the VIX rises, and a bill moving in Congress would make tech companies pay those energy costs (CNBC, [Jun 24]).
Reported: UK multi-utility supplier Telecom Plus fell 25% on its profit outlook and a dividend cut (Sharecast.com, [Jun 23]).
EPS Upside Watch: Bloom Energy — the supplier of on-site fuel-cell power to data centres could be worth $920 after a deal expansion (TIKR.com, [Jun 26]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: Caught between EV-transition costs, Chinese competition and tariff risk, the sector's driver is China, where German automakers' superprofit margins are vanishing (Automotive News, [Jun 25]), so cost cuts such as Volkswagen's plan for up to 100,000 job cuts (New York Post, [Jun 26]) carry the earnings story.

Reported: BMW prepares worker talks after a profit warning and China slowdown (The Manufacturer, [Jun 25]); its 1-3% profit margin is a 'wake-up call' for the industry facing Chinese competition (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 26]). Porsche's CEO stuck to targets on the road to recovery (Reuters, [Jun 22]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged.
